q: A classmate writes: "The Unit 3 empires rose because the Mongols handed them their lands." Which correction is most accurate?
opts: The Mongols were still the strongest power in all of Asia in 1500
The Mongol breakup left a vacuum new states filled
The Unit 3 empires were all founded by Mongol khans
The Unit 3 empires conquered the Mongols at their peak
why: Mongol power had collapsed by then.
Only the Mughals had Mongol ancestry, through Babur.
They rose after the Mongols fell apart.

q: A sultan's army breaks through city walls that had stood for centuries by firing massive bronze cannons. Which development does this show?
opts: Gunpowder drove imperial expansion
Religious tolerance won over conquered peoples
Tribute systems funded imperial armies
Maritime empires replaced land empires in Asia
why: Cannons are military, not religious policy.
This is about weapons, not revenue.
This is a land siege, not a sea empire.

q: A North African army crosses the Sahara in 1591 and defeats a larger West African army with firearms. What best explains the invasion?
opts: The invaders wanted to spread Shi'a Islam
The invaders were fleeing the Ottoman army
The invaders wanted the gold trade routes
The West Africans had attacked Spain first
exp: Morocco took on Songhai to control the gold trade.
why: Both states were Sunni Muslim.
The goal was gold, not escape.
No such attack happened.

q: Two Muslim empires, one Sunni and one Shi'a, fight a major battle in 1514 in northwestern Iran. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: The Safavids beat the Ottomans at Panipat
The Mughals beat the Safavids at Kandahar
The Ottomans beat the Mamluks at Chaldiran
Ottomans beat Safavids at Chaldiran
exp: Chaldiran: Sunni Ottomans versus Shi'a Safavids.
why: Panipat was Babur's battle in India in 1526.
Kandahar changed hands later, in the 1600s.
The Mamluks fell in 1516–1517 in Egypt and Syria.

q: Which statement best compares the two rivalries of the Safavid Empire, according to your textbook?
opts: Religion mattered more in the Ottoman war
Religion caused both rivalries equally and nothing else mattered
Neither rivalry involved any religious disagreement
The Safavids fought both rivals mainly over the gold of Timbuktu
exp: Watch-out: the Safavid–Mughal war centered on Kandahar and trade.
why: AMSCO says the Mughal war was mainly about resources and trade routes.
The Ottoman–Safavid rivalry was strongly religious.
Timbuktu was in West Africa.

q: An emperor lets local landholders collect taxes from peasants and keep a share as payment. Which empire and system?
opts: Mughal zamindars
Ottoman tax farming
Mexica tribute lists
The Ming Single Whip
exp: Zamindars kept a share of the land tax.
why: Ottoman tax farmers bid for the right to collect and paid a fixed sum up front.
Tribute came from conquered provinces.
That combined taxes into one silver payment.

q: A government orders that land taxes and labor duties be combined and paid in silver. Which state?
opts: Ming China
Safavid Persia under Shah Abbas I
Tokugawa Japan under the shoguns
Russia under Peter the Great
why: The Safavids are not linked to this reform.
Japan supplied silver; the reform was Chinese.
Peter introduced a head tax in 1718.

q: A French king builds an enormous palace, decorates it with sun imagery and makes his court revolve around him. What is he doing?
opts: Using tax farming to raise money
Using the devshirme to train officials
Using religious tolerance to win support
Using architecture to legitimize rule
exp: Versailles: monumental architecture plus control of nobles.
why: The palace is about display and control.
That is Ottoman.
This is about the king's glory, not tolerance.

q: A shogun requires every regional lord to keep a home in the capital and leave his family there when he is away. What is the main goal?
opts: Encouraging trade with Portugal
Training lords as Christian priests
Preventing lords from rebelling
Collecting tribute from China
exp: Alternate attendance kept the daimyo under control.
why: The policy is about lords, not foreign trade.
The Tokugawa banned Christianity.
Japan did not collect tribute from China.

q: Which pair shows two rulers creating elites loyal only to themselves rather than to nobles?
opts: The Taj Mahal and Versailles
The devshirme and the oprichnina
The Peace of Augsburg and Westphalia
The jizya and the head tax
exp: Ottoman and Russian rulers bypassed the nobility.
why: Those are buildings, not elites.
Those are religious settlements.
Those are taxes.

q: A monk criticizes the sale of indulgences and argues that Scripture outranks Church hierarchy. What movement does he start?
opts: The Protestant break
The Counter-Reformation
Sikhism in the Punjab region of South Asia
The Scientific Revolution
why: That was the Catholic response.
Sikhism grew in the Punjab.
That was based on reason and evidence, not Scripture.

q: A Catholic council meets from 1545 to 1563 to reaffirm Church doctrine. Which statement about it is accurate?
opts: It started the Protestant Reformation
It ended the Thirty Years' War in Germany
It made Calvinism a legal choice
It was part of the Catholic response
why: Luther started that in 1517.
Westphalia ended that war in 1648.
Westphalia did that.

q: A faith in the Punjab rejects caste, teaches devotion to one God and grows amid Hindu–Muslim interaction. Which statement is accurate?
opts: It was imposed by the Safavid shahs
It is an example of syncretism
It began as a branch of Shi'a Islam
It was founded by Akbar as Din-i Ilahi
why: It grew from contact, not imposition.
It is a separate faith.
Akbar's faith was different and unpopular.

q: A new Iranian dynasty makes Twelver Shi'ism the official faith, alarming its powerful Sunni neighbor. Name both empires.
opts: Mughals of India and Ottomans
Ottomans and Mamluks
Safavids and Ottomans
Safavids and Qing
why: The Mughals ruled India, not Iran.
Neither is the Iranian dynasty.
The Qing were not the Sunni neighbor of Iran.

q: Akbar ended the tax on non-Muslims; Aurangzeb restored it. Which theme does this comparison best show?
opts: Change in religious policy within one empire
Continuity in Mughal tolerance across 150 years
The spread of Christianity into India by force
Competition between land and sea empires
exp: Akbar vs. Aurangzeb: tolerance vs. strict Sunni rule.
why: The policy reversed; that is change.
The tax concerned Hindus and other non-Muslims.
This is internal religious policy.

q: Foreign rulers kept China's Confucian exam but required Han men to wear their own hairstyle. What does this show?
opts: They rejected all Chinese traditions
They fully assimilated into Han culture
They ruled through religious tolerance only
They adapted while asserting control
why: They kept the exam and the Mandate of Heaven.
The queue kept a Manchu marker of control.
The queue was imposed.

q: Which empire was LEAST centralized, according to your textbook?
opts: The Ottoman Empire, with its devshirme officials
The Aztecs, who relied on tribute and fear
The Qing Empire, with its exam-chosen officials
The Inca Empire, with its decimal provinces
exp: The Aztecs controlled Mesoamerica through force rather than bureaucracy.
why: The devshirme created a centralized bureaucracy.
The exam supported a strong bureaucracy.
AMSCO calls the Inca very organized.

q: Your textbook explains why Russia outlasted the three Islamic gunpowder empires. Which explanation fits it best?
opts: Russia avoided war with its neighbors
Russia converted to Islam to unify its people
Russia modernized its army on Western models
Russia had no need for firearms in Siberia
why: Russia fought often.
Russia stayed Orthodox Christian.
Cossacks used firearms in Siberia.
